Sup A: bolton_2006_cake_intermediate_blocking · Combined models of membrane fouling: Development and application to microfiltration and ultrafiltration of biological fluids (Cake-intermediate blocking)
The cake-intermediate blocking model describes fouling during filtration of biological fluids through microporous or virus-retention membranes. It predicts permeate volume over time during constant-pressure operation and pressure rise over time during constant-flow operation. The model combines loss of available membrane area through intermediate blocking with increasing flow resistance from cake formation, using Darcy’s law to derive explicit time-dependent equations. The authors evaluated it with human plasma IgG filtered through Durapore PVDF membranes and BSA filtered through Viresolve 180 membranes, under both constant-pressure and constant-flow conditions. They fitted two parameters by minimizing squared residuals and compared its predictions with individual and other combined fouling models.
availability: The paper does not state whether the model code or experimental data are publicly available.
comparison: The authors describe their combined models as less physically detailed but simpler to implement than the Ho and Zydney model, which used three fitted parameters.
comparison: The combined-model development extends the earlier pore-blockage and cake-filtration model of Ho and Zydney (2000).
comparison: The model’s individual blocking and cake-filtration components follow the established blocking-filtration and cake-filtration laws discussed by Grace (1956) and Hermia (1982).
data: Five constant-pressure BSA runs were performed, and the reported curve and error bars show the average and one standard deviation across runs.
data: The BSA filtration measurements continued until flux had fallen 98% from its initial value.
data: Three constant-flow IgG experiments measured pressure over time in 47 mm holders.
data: Three constant-pressure IgG experiments were performed in 13 mm holders, and measurements continued until flux had fallen 95% from its initial value.

equations: At constant pressure, the model predicts permeate volume as a function of time.
equipment: Constant-pressure filtration used 13 or 47 mm stainless-steel membrane holders.
equipment: The constant-pressure system used a pressurized vessel, an electronic balance with a load cell, and a digital pressure gauge.
fitting: For constant-flow IgG, the authors fitted the models to one experiment and reported that the other two experiments were similar.
fitting: Model fits were assessed by minimizing the sum of squared residuals between observations and model predictions.

materials: The IgG feed was human plasma IgG at 10.0 mg/mL in pH 7.2 PBS buffer.

measurement: The constant-pressure data-acquisition system recorded measurements every second for one hour.
mechanism: Cake filtration represents particles accumulating on the membrane surface in a growing permeable layer that adds flow resistance.
mechanism: In the intermediate-blocking law, available membrane area decreases exponentially with processed permeate volume.
mechanism: Intermediate blocking represents particles sealing some pores while other particles accumulate on previously deposited particles.
mechanism: The cake-filtration law represents increasing resistance as processed volume increases.

membrane: The IgG tests used Durapore PVDF membranes with a nominal pore-size rating of 0.22 μm.

model: The model is built from Darcy’s law and gives explicit time-dependent predictions for both constant-pressure and constant-flow operation.
model: The model represents fouling as a reduction in available filtration area together with an increase in filtration resistance.
model: The paper presents algebraic time-dependent equations rather than a spatially resolved description of the membrane.

operation: Constant-pressure IgG tests were run at 10 psi.

parameters: The paper reports fitted parameter estimates but does not report parameter confidence intervals or other uncertainty estimates.
results: For constant-flow IgG, the cake-intermediate model had an SSR of 0.58, lower than the cake-complete model’s 1.36 and the cake-standard model’s 13.5.
results: For constant-flow IgG, the three combined models fit substantially better than the individual fouling models.
results: For constant-pressure BSA, the cake-intermediate and cake-complete fits were within the standard deviation of most data points.
results: For constant-pressure BSA, the cake-intermediate model had an SSR of 9.59 × 10², slightly lower than the cake-complete model’s 1.62 × 10³.
results: For constant-pressure IgG, the individual intermediate-blocking model fit about as well as the combined cake-intermediate model.
results: The authors’ parameter-based comparison indicated that caking was a major component of the cake-intermediate fit for constant-flow IgG.

Sup B: bolton_2006_intermediate_standard_blocking · Combined models of membrane fouling: Development and application to microfiltration and ultrafiltration of biological fluids (Intermediate-standard blocking)
The Intermediate-standard blocking model represents protein fouling of microporous membranes by combining intermediate blocking, which reduces the available pore area, with standard blocking, which constricts pores and raises filtration resistance. Based on Darcy’s law, it predicts filtrate volume over time during constant-pressure filtration and pressure rise over time during constant-flow filtration using two fitted parameters. The paper tested it on human IgG filtration through a 0.22 μm PVDF membrane and BSA filtration through a virus-retention membrane, including constant-pressure and constant-flow runs. Model curves were fitted to measured filtration profiles by minimizing the sum of squared residuals. In the tested cases, this combined model did not improve on the relevant individual blocking model, and the authors describe it as applicable when the combined mechanisms match observed fouling.
comparison: The earlier Ho and Zydney (2000) model used three fitted parameters and required numerical integration for volume- or pressure-time predictions.
comparison: The paper cites Grace (1956) for standard-blocking background and Hermia (1982) for standard, complete, and intermediate blocking laws.
comparison: The paper compares its combined models with the more physically detailed combined blockage-and-cake model of Ho and Zydney (2000), noting that the new models are simpler to implement.

formulation: The combined model reduces to its component individual models when one mechanism dominates.

measurement: The BSA filtration results were averaged across five runs, with standard deviations calculated at each time point.
measurement: The constant-pressure setup recorded data every second for one hour.
mechanisms: In the combined model, intermediate blocking reduces available membrane area while standard blocking increases filtration resistance.
mechanisms: Intermediate blocking represents some particles sealing pores while other deposited particles accumulate on top of them.
mechanisms: Standard blocking represents deposits constricting straight cylindrical membrane pores.
membrane: The BSA virus-filtration tests used Viresolve 180, a PVDF composite with a thin ultraporous layer over a thicker microporous layer.
membrane: The IgG sterile-filtration tests used 0.22 μm nominal-pore-size Durapore PVDF membranes.
model: Intermediate-standard blocking is one of the five combined fouling models developed in the paper.
model: The model is expressed through algebraic time relationships rather than a state-based dynamic system.
operation: Constant-pressure tests used 10 psi for Durapore membranes and 30 psi for Viresolve 180 membranes.
parameters: The model uses two fitted parameters, the intermediate-blocking constant and the standard-blocking constant.
prediction: The model predicts permeate volume over time for constant-pressure operation and pressure over time for constant-flow operation.
results: For constant-flow IgG, the intermediate-standard model fitted as well as the intermediate-blocking model alone.
results: For constant-pressure BSA, the intermediate-standard model produced the same fit as the intermediate-blocking model alone.
results: For constant-pressure IgG, the intermediate-standard model fitted no better than the standard-blocking model alone.
scope: The authors say the combined models involving standard blocking do not cover as broad a range of flux-decline behavior as the cake-complete model.
scope: The paper presents the combined standard-and-intermediate equations as applicable when fouling is observed to involve that specific combination of mechanisms.
use: The authors position intermediate-standard blocking as a candidate for describing fouling when the combined mechanisms agree with experimental observations, rather than as a broadly useful general-purpose fit.
validation: The paper reports fitting the model to experimental profiles but does not describe a separate held-out validation data set.

answer.description: A and B are alternative combined fouling models from the same study, tested on the same IgG and BSA filtration systems under constant-pressure and constant-flow operation. Both combine intermediate blocking, which reduces available membrane area, with another mechanism, and use Darcy’s law and two fitted parameters to predict filtration profiles. A combines intermediate blocking with cake filtration, adding resistance from a growing surface layer; B combines it with standard blocking, which constricts pores. Their reported fit comparisons differ: A improved on its component models in some cases, while B fitted no better than the relevant individual blocking model in the tested cases.
